exercises.prompt: A 60 kg humanoid walks at $1.0$ m/s with a cost of transport of $0.8$ (electrical energy per unit weight per unit distance). Taking $g = 9.81$ m/s², how many **watts** does walking draw, to the nearest watt?

feedback.message: Not yet. You multiplied the cost of transport by the mass and speed but forgot $g$: the definition uses weight, $mg$.
Not yet. That is $mgv$ alone. Multiply by the cost of transport, $0.8$.

hints: The cost of transport is $c = P/(mgv)$, so $P = c\,m g v$.
exercises.solution: $P = c\,m g v = 0.8 \times 60 \times 9.81 \times 1.0 = 470.9$ W, about **471 W**. A person of the same mass at a metabolic cost of transport of about $0.2$ would spend roughly a quarter of that. Add a GPU module, sensors and the arms, and a walking humanoid easily draws 600–1,000 W, which is why most 2026 deployments keep walking distances short.

exercises.prompt: A humanoid has a 2.0 kWh battery, of which 90% is usable. On a delivery route it draws 450 W for walking, 120 W for its computer and 30 W for everything else. How many **minutes** can it work before it must recharge?

feedback.message: Not yet. Only 90% of the 2.0 kWh is usable: 1,800 Wh, not 2,000 Wh.
Not yet. You used only the walking power. The computer and other loads draw power too: 600 W in all.
That is the runtime in hours. The question asks for minutes.

hints: Total power is the sum of the loads; runtime is energy divided by power.
exercises.solution: Usable energy $= 0.9 \times 2000 = 1800$ Wh. Total power $= 450 + 120 + 30 = 600$ W. Runtime $= 1800/600 = 3$ h $=$ **180 minutes**. In practice the runtime is shorter still, because battery capacity falls with age and cold, and peaks of power (climbing, lifting) cost more than the average suggests.

exercises.prompt: Many legged robots use **quasi-direct-drive** actuators (a large motor with a gear ratio of about 6–10:1) in their legs rather than compact motors with 100:1 strain-wave gears. What is the main reason?

options.label: Low gear ratios keep the joint backdrivable and its reflected inertia small, so the leg can absorb foot impacts and sense forces through motor current
options.feedback: Yes. Reflected inertia grows with the square of the ratio, and a backdrivable joint 'gives' on impact instead of shocking the gearbox; force sensing comes almost free.

options.label: They make less heat when holding a load
options.feedback: Not yet. The lesson's table showed the opposite: at a low ratio the motor must supply more torque, and heat grows with its square (57 W against 11 W for the 100:1 joint).

options.label: They are lighter for the same torque
options.feedback: Not quite. A low ratio needs a larger, heavier motor to reach the same joint torque; that is the price paid for the dynamic benefits.

options.label: Strain-wave gears cannot be used in robots
options.feedback: Not yet. Strain-wave gears are everywhere in robot arms and in many humanoid wrists and arms; they are compact and precise, but stiff and less tolerant of shock.

hints: What happens to a gearbox when a 70 kg robot's foot hits the ground?
How does the rotor's inertia appear at the joint through a gearbox of ratio $N$?
exercises.solution: **(a).** Through a gearbox of ratio $N$, a rotor of inertia $J$ appears at the joint as $N^2 J$: 100:1 multiplies it by 10,000, 9:1 by 81. Each foot strike must decelerate that inertia, and a stiff, highly geared joint passes the shock to its teeth. A low-ratio joint is backdrivable, so the leg behaves like a controllable spring and the motor current tells the controller how hard the foot is pushing. The costs are a heavier motor and more heat when holding still, which is why designers use different actuators at different joints.

exercises.prompt: A fenced industrial arm is made safe by cutting power to its motors and engaging brakes. Why is this **not** an adequate safe state for a walking humanoid?

options.label: Without powered balance it falls as an inverted pendulum within about a second or two, releasing hundreds of joules
options.feedback: Yes. The lesson's model put a 70 kg robot on the ground 1.1–1.9 s after losing power, releasing about 650 J. Its stop must be a controlled crouch or kneel while still powered.

options.label: Humanoids have no brakes
options.feedback: Not quite. Some humanoid joints do have brakes, but locking every joint of a standing robot does not stop it toppling as a rigid body about its feet.

options.label: Cutting power would erase the robot's learned policy
options.feedback: Not yet. Policies are stored in non-volatile memory; the problem is mechanical, not software.

options.label: Industrial standards forbid emergency stops on mobile robots
options.feedback: Not yet. Emergency stops are required; the question is what the robot does when one is pressed.

hints: Think of a broom balanced on your palm, and what happens if you stop moving your hand.
exercises.solution: **(a).** A standing humanoid is an inverted pendulum with a time constant $\sqrt{L/g} \approx 0.3$ s for a centre of mass about 1 m high. Remove active balance and any small tilt grows exponentially; the robot hits the ground in one to two seconds, possibly onto a person. Its safe stop must therefore be a powered, controlled transition to a stable posture, then power-off. This is precisely the gap the draft standard ISO 25785-1 for actively balancing industrial mobile robots is meant to fill; existing standards such as ISO 10218 assume a robot that stays put when stopped.

exercises.prompt: Write two functions for an electric joint with gear ratio `ratio`, gearbox efficiency `eta` and motor constant `km` (N m per square-root watt). `joint_heat(load_torque, ratio, eta, km)` returns the Joule heat in watts while statically holding `load_torque` at the joint, using motor torque $\tau_m = \tau / (N\eta)$ and heat $(\tau_m / K_m)^2$. `max_hold_torque(ratio, eta, km, heat_limit)` returns the largest joint torque that can be held indefinitely without exceeding `heat_limit` watts.
exercises.starter:
import math

def joint_heat(load_torque, ratio, eta, km):
    """Watts of Joule heat while holding load_torque (N m) at the joint."""
    return 0.0

def max_hold_torque(ratio, eta, km, heat_limit):
    """Largest joint torque (N m) that keeps the heat at or below heat_limit (W)."""
    return 0.0
exercises.tests:
import math
assert math.isclose(joint_heat(38.0, 9, 0.93, 0.60), 57.26, rel_tol=1e-3), f"quasi-direct-drive shoulder from the lesson: expected about 57.3 W, got {joint_heat(38.0, 9, 0.93, 0.60)}"
assert math.isclose(joint_heat(38.0, 100, 0.75, 0.15), 11.41, rel_tol=1e-3), "strain-wave 100:1 joint: about 11.4 W"
assert math.isclose(joint_heat(0.0, 50, 0.8, 0.15), 0.0), "no load, no heat"
assert math.isclose(joint_heat(20.0, 10, 1.0, 1.0) * 4, joint_heat(40.0, 10, 1.0, 1.0)), "heat grows with the square of the torque"
t = max_hold_torque(9, 0.93, 0.60, 53.3)
assert math.isclose(t, 36.66, rel_tol=1e-3), f"expected about 36.7 N m, got {t}"
assert math.isclose(joint_heat(t, 9, 0.93, 0.60), 53.3, rel_tol=1e-9), "the two functions must be inverses"
hints: First the motor torque: divide the joint torque by `ratio * eta`.
Invert: `motor_torque = km * sqrt(heat_limit)`, then multiply by `ratio * eta`.

exercises.prompt: Write `cost_per_hour(price, years, hours_per_year, maintenance_frac, power_kw, energy_price)`, the cost of one working hour of a robot: its purchase price spread evenly over its working life, plus yearly maintenance (a fraction of the price each year) spread over the year's working hours, plus electricity. All money is in the same currency unit.
exercises.tests:
import math
c = cost_per_hour(100000, 5, 4000, 0.10, 0.5, 0.15)
assert math.isclose(c, 7.575), f"expected 5.0 depreciation + 2.5 maintenance + 0.075 energy = 7.575, got {c}"
c2 = cost_per_hour(100000, 5, 2000, 0.10, 0.5, 0.15)
assert math.isclose(c2, 15.075), f"half the working hours roughly doubles the fixed costs per hour; expected 15.075, got {c2}"
assert math.isclose(cost_per_hour(0, 5, 4000, 0.1, 1.0, 0.2), 0.2), "a free robot still costs its electricity"
exercises.reference:
def cost_per_hour(price, years, hours_per_year, maintenance_frac, power_kw, energy_price):
    depreciation = price / (years * hours_per_year)
    maintenance = maintenance_frac * price / hours_per_year
    energy = power_kw * energy_price
    return depreciation + maintenance + energy
hints: Depreciation per hour is the price divided by the total working hours, `years * hours_per_year`.
Maintenance per hour is `maintenance_frac * price / hours_per_year`.
Energy per hour is `power_kw * energy_price` (kilowatt-hours per hour times price per kilowatt-hour).
exercises.solution:
```python
def cost_per_hour(price, years, hours_per_year, maintenance_frac, power_kw, energy_price):
    depreciation = price / (years * hours_per_year)
    maintenance = maintenance_frac * price / hours_per_year
    energy = power_kw * energy_price
    return depreciation + maintenance + energy
```

With a price of 100,000, a five-year life at 4,000 hours a year (two shifts), 10% maintenance a year, 0.5 kW and an electricity price of 0.15 per kWh, an hour costs $5.0 + 2.5 + 0.075 = 7.575$ units. Two things stand out. Electricity is almost irrelevant; utilisation is everything — at 2,000 hours a year the cost per hour doubles. And this model leaves out what often dominates in practice: integration engineering, supervision, downtime, and the robot's speed relative to the task, since a robot that works at half a person's pace needs twice the hours for the same output.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about humanoid robots are accurate **as of 2026**? Select all that apply.

options.label: Figure reported that Figure 02 robots worked about eleven months on a BMW line in South Carolina, loading parts for more than 30,000 cars
options.feedback: Yes. Figure published this in November 2025, including that the forearm was the most common hardware failure.

options.label: Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada signed an agreement in 2026 to deploy Agility Robotics' Digit
options.feedback: Yes, in February 2026, for seven robots unloading parts totes, under a robots-as-a-service arrangement.

options.label: A published ISO standard certifies humanoids to work freely alongside people in factories
options.feedback: Not yet. The standard for actively balancing industrial mobile robots, ISO 25785-1, was still a draft in 2026; most deployments separate humanoids from people.

options.label: More humanoids are installed each year than conventional industrial robot arms
options.feedback: Not yet. About 542,000 industrial robots were installed in 2024 (IFR); humanoid shipments were in the tens of thousands a year.

options.label: By analysts' estimates, most humanoids shipped in 2025 and early 2026 were built by Chinese companies
options.feedback: Yes. Several estimates put the share above 90%, led by AgiBot and Unitree.

hints: Compare the scale of humanoid shipments with the IFR's yearly count of industrial robots.
Was the dedicated standard for balancing robots published or still a draft?
exercises.solution: **a, b and e.** Deployments in 2026 are real but small: a few robots per site, one or two tasks each, at BMW, Toyota Canada, GXO and others, with Chinese companies building most of the units shipped. Statement (c) is false — ISO 25785-1 was a committee draft — and (d) is false by more than an order of magnitude: conventional industrial robots are installed at about half a million a year.
